properties.notes: The civic, religious, and commercial heart of Rome since the archaic period; by 117 CE it was ringed by the Curia, basilicas, temples, and the Rostra. Point marks the representative centroid of the forum valley between the Capitoline and Palatine.

Third permanent Senate House on this site, begun by Julius Caesar in 44 BCE to replace the Curia Cornelia/Hostilia, completed and dedicated by Augustus in 29 BCE; rebuilt again after a fire under Domitian c. 94 CE. Standing and in use as the meeting hall of the Senate in 117 CE. Survives today largely intact because it was converted into the church of Sant'Adriano in 630 CE.

Civil law-court basilica on the south side of the Forum, begun by Caesar in 54 BCE, dedicated unfinished in 46 BCE, completed by Augustus and rededicated in 12 CE to Gaius and Lucius Caesar after a fire. Housed the centumviral court; standing in 117 CE (it burned again only in 283 CE under Carinus).

North side of the Forum, opposite the Basilica Julia; first built by the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior in 179 BCE, rebuilt after fires under Augustus (14 BCE) and again after a fire in 22 CE under Tiberius, with continuing Julio-Claudian era repairs. Pliny (NH 36.24) counted it among the most beautiful buildings in the world; standing in 117 CE (it was finally destroyed by the Visigothic sack of 410 CE).

One of the oldest temples in the Forum, dedicated 497 BCE at the foot of the Capitoline; rebuilt by L. Munatius Plancus c. 42 BCE. Doubled as the state treasury (Aerarium Populi Romani), standing and functioning as such in 117 CE (the surviving columned facade dates from a later, post-283 CE, rebuild).

Round temple housing Rome's sacred hearth-fire, tended by the Vestal Virgins; rebuilt repeatedly after fires (most famously by Augustus c. 12 BCE, and later again under Julia Domna in 191 CE, after our snapshot date). The 117 CE-era structure was the Augustan-period rebuild; in continuous cult use.

Residence of the six Vestal Virgins adjoining the Temple of Vesta; the building visible today is largely a 2nd-century CE Hadrianic/Trajanic-era rebuild replacing earlier structures. Occupied and in continuous use in 117 CE.

Vowed 499/496 BCE after the Battle of Lake Regillus, dedicated 484 BCE; rebuilt by Tiberius after a fire, rededicated 6 CE in the names of Tiberius and his late brother Drusus. Standing in 117 CE; three Corinthian columns of this Tiberian rebuild survive today.

Built on the site of Julius Caesar's funeral pyre, authorized by the Second Triumvirate in 42 BCE and dedicated by Augustus on 18 August 29 BCE; the first temple in Rome dedicated to a deified mortal Roman. Standing in 117 CE.

Original temple vowed 367 BCE, rebuilt 121 BCE by L. Opimius; completely rebuilt on a larger scale by the future emperor Tiberius between 7 BCE and 10 CE and rededicated as the Aedes Concordiae Augustae on 16 January 10 CE. This Tiberian-era temple was standing at the west end of the Forum in 117 CE.

Traditionally the residence of the kings of Rome, later the official headquarters of the Pontifex Maximus and seat of the pontifical archives; rebuilt in stone/marble after a fire in 36 BCE by Cn. Domitius Calvinus. Standing and functioning as the pontifical office in 117 CE (in this period the emperor himself held the office of Pontifex Maximus).

Public oratory platform at the northwest end of the Forum square, decorated with captured ships' prows (rostra); rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE as a curved 'hemicycle' and extended by Augustus with a rectangular marble-faced platform c. 24 m wide. In active use for public speeches in 117 CE. Coordinates are approximate (no precisely surveyed findspot published for the platform's exact footprint independent of later Severan-era rebuilding).

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy, Via Sacra, Roman Forum
properties.notes: Triumphal arch on the Via Sacra commemorating the deified Titus and the joint Flavian victory in the Jewish War (70 CE); erected by Domitian shortly after Titus's death, c. 81-82 CE. Standing in 117 CE; famous for its relief panels of the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple.

Chief state temple of Rome atop the Capitoline, originally dedicated 509 BCE; destroyed and rebuilt three times (83 BCE fire, Vitellian-era fire 69 CE, Titus-era fire 80 CE), with the final Domitianic reconstruction in gleaming Pentelic marble dedicated c. 82 CE. This was the temple standing in 117 CE, the terminus of every triumphal procession.

Rome's public records office, built into the Capitoline slope above the Forum, ordered under Sulla and completed 78 BCE by consul Q. Lutatius Catulus following the fire of 83 BCE. Standing and in use in 117 CE; its lower arcades survive intact within the modern Capitoline Museums.

Private residential wing of Domitian's vast Flavian imperial palace on the Palatine, completed 92 CE by his architect Rabirius; from this point the main imperial residence of Rome through the 2nd century. In use as the emperor's palace in 117 CE (Trajan died in Cilicia, but Rome's imperial household still resided here).

Official/public wing of Domitian's Palatine palace complex (audience hall, basilica, triclinium, and a large peristyle with an octagonal island fountain), completed 92 CE, architect Rabirius. Standing and in use for imperial ceremony and state banquets in 117 CE.

Rome's great chariot-racing stadium in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine, traditionally founded under the kings; rebuilt in stone/monumentalized under Julius Caesar and Augustus, and rebuilt again by Trajan after a fire under Domitian, with Trajan's reconstruction completed c. 103 CE. This Trajanic-era Circus, capable of holding well over 150,000 spectators, was in full use in 117 CE.

Rome's great amphitheater, begun under Vespasian on the drained lake of Nero's Domus Aurea, dedicated by Titus in 80 CE with 100 days of games, and completed with a fourth story added by Domitian c. 82 CE. Fully standing and hosting spectacles in 117 CE.

Last and largest of the Imperial Fora, built with the spoils of the Dacian Wars, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus, construction begun c. 105-107 CE and formally dedicated 112 CE; the Basilica Ulpia, twin libraries, and Column followed by 113 CE. Newly completed and the showpiece of the city in 117 CE.

Multi-level complex of shops, offices, and market halls built into the excavated Quirinal slope beside Trajan's Forum, constructed c. 100-110 CE by Apollodorus of Damascus, inaugurated 113 CE. Fully functioning commercial complex in 117 CE.

38 m (with pedestal) freestanding marble victory column between the Basilica Ulpia and the twin libraries, its shaft wrapped in a continuous helical relief depicting the Dacian Wars; dedicated 12 May 113 CE. Newly erected and gleaming in 117 CE; Trajan's ashes were interred in its base after his death in August 117.

Twin library halls (one Latin, one Greek), each holding an estimated 20,000 scrolls, flanking Trajan's Column within the Forum of Trajan; founded by Trajan c. 114 CE. One of the great libraries of the ancient world, newly opened and functioning in 117 CE. Coordinates approximate the space between the Basilica Ulpia and the Temple of the Deified Trajan.

The first of Rome's monumental 'imperial' bath complexes, built on the Oppian Hill over part of the buried Domus Aurea; designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and formally inaugurated on 22 June (Kalends of July) 109 CE. Covering roughly 330 x 340 m, it was operating at full scale in 117 CE.

Public bath complex built quickly by Titus and dedicated in 80 or 81 CE alongside the newly opened Colosseum, incorporating part of Nero's former Domus Aurea. One of the earliest 'imperial thermae' establishing the symmetrical plan later copied at the Baths of Trajan next door; still in operation in 117 CE, though already overshadowed by Trajan's larger complex.

Public baths in the Campus Martius near the Pantheon and Saepta, built by Nero c. 62-64 CE (the earliest of Rome's grand imperial thermae, predating even Titus's); listed among the notable buildings of the city by Martial and later authors. Still standing and in use in 117 CE under its original name (it was only enlarged and renamed Thermae Alexandrinae after Severus Alexander's restoration in the 3rd century).

COMPLICATED CASE - marked NOT extant/complete as of August 117 CE, deliberately, per snapshot rules. Agrippa's original rectangular Pantheon (27 BCE) burned in the great fire of 80 CE; Domitian's rebuild burned again after a lightning strike, per Cassius Dio 66.24 (dated to 110 CE under Trajan). Brick-stamp analysis by Lise Hetland ('Dating the Pantheon', JRA 2007) argues the great rotunda now standing was begun by Trajan shortly after the 110 CE fire, with site clearance and material orders underway by c. 114 CE, and was structurally advanced but very likely still an active construction site at Trajan's death in August 117 -- Hadrian (who acceded 11 August 117) gets conventional credit for the building and it was not dedicated until after 125 CE. Because it was not a complete, functioning temple on 8 August 117 CE, extant_117ce is set false; kept on the map (per project guardrails for commissioned-but-unfinished works) flagged as an active building site at the moment of the snapshot.
sources: Lise Hetland, 'Dating the Pantheon', Journal of Roman Archaeology 20 (2007), summarized at https://erenow.org/ancient/the-pantheon-from-antiquity-to-the-present/3.php

properties.notes: Permanent stone theater begun by Julius Caesar and completed/dedicated by Augustus in 13 BCE, named for his deceased nephew and heir-apparent Marcellus; one of the earliest permanent theaters in Rome, seating roughly 11,000-20,000. Standing and in use in 117 CE.

Open consecrated ground in the southern Campus Martius, laid out by censor Gaius Flaminius in 221 BCE; unlike the Circus Maximus it was never a fully enclosed monumental racetrack, functioning more as a public square used for games, assemblies, and triumphal musters, surrounded over time by temples and porticoes (e.g. Porticus Octaviae). Still an active open space in 117 CE. Its exact perimeter is not archaeologically fixed, so the point is an approximate centroid.

Vast circular tomb (90 m diameter, c. 42 m tall) built by Augustus in 28 BCE in the northern Campus Martius as the dynastic tomb for himself and the Julio-Claudian family, planted with cypresses and topped by his statue. Standing and receiving imperial burials (it remained the resting place of the Julio-Claudians and was still an active monument, though Trajan himself was interred instead at the base of his own Column) in 117 CE.

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy, right bank of the Tiber
properties.notes: NOT standing in 117 CE - included on the map anyway (per project guardrails for a site of major later significance under construction near the snapshot date) because Hadrian's accession is literally the event that closes this snapshot (Trajan died 8 August 117; Hadrian, acclaimed emperor days later, is traditionally credited as planner of this tomb). Brick-stamp evidence gives a terminus post quem of 123 CE for construction, with most scholarship favoring an actual building start c. 125-130 CE; it was completed and dedicated only in 139 CE under Antoninus Pius, after Hadrian's own death. In August 117 CE this was simply open ground on the right bank of the Tiber -- no construction had yet begun.

properties.modern_location: Rome, Italy (original site near Piazza San Lorenzo in Lucina; monument now displayed ~350m away near the Mausoleum of Augustus)
properties.notes: Marble altar within a sculpted precinct wall commemorating the Pax Romana established by Augustus, commissioned by the Senate in 13 BCE and consecrated 30 January 9 BCE, sited on the west side of the Via Flaminia in the Campus Martius. Standing and in cult use in 117 CE. Coordinates mark the approximate ancient findspot beneath the later Palazzo Fiano-Almagia (excavated 1937-38); the monument was moved and reassembled at its current Richard Meier museum site near Augustus's Mausoleum only in the 20th century.

NOT extant as a functioning palace in 117 CE - kept on the map for context because it directly underlies two extant POIs. Nero's sprawling post-fire palace complex (64 CE) was disowned by the Flavians: its lake was drained for the Colosseum, and its Esquiline wing was deliberately buried under earthen fill to serve as the foundation for the Baths of Titus (80 CE) and then the much larger Baths of Trajan (104-109 CE). By 117 CE the site was entirely subsumed beneath Trajan's bathing complex; the buried frescoed halls survived underground and were not rediscovered until the Renaissance.

properties.name_latin: Aquae Claudia et Anio Novus (ad Portam Maiorem)
properties.name_english: Aqua Claudia / Anio Novus crossing at Porta Maggiore
properties.notes: Monumental double-arched travertine structure built by Claudius in 52 CE to carry the Aqua Claudia and (stacked above it) the Anio Novus aqueduct channels across the Via Praenestina and Via Labicana as they entered the city; restored under Vespasian and Titus. This arched aqueduct crossing was fully functional in 117 CE, supplying two of Rome's principal aqueducts (it was only incorporated as a city gate, Porta Maggiore, into the Aurelian Walls in the 270s CE, after our snapshot).

properties.name_english: Aqua Virgo terminus (later site of the Trevi Fountain)
properties.notes: Aqueduct completed by Agrippa in 19 BCE, running c. 20.5 km mostly underground from springs east of Rome, built specifically to feed Agrippa's Baths and the pools/canal (Euripus) of the Campus Martius. Fully operational and delivering water into central Rome in 117 CE; its terminal distribution point in antiquity lay near where the Baroque Trevi Fountain now stands (the fountain itself is an 18th-century addition, included here only to mark the ancient terminus location).

Rome's first purpose-built imperial harbor at the Tiber mouth, begun by Claudius in 42 CE to supplement the silting river-mouth port at Ostia; two long curving moles enclosed roughly 200 ha of open water, with an artificial mole-top island carrying the Pharos at the seaward entrance. Nero completed associated works and issued sestertii celebrating the harbor's operation at its ceremonial opening in 64 CE. Exposed to open-sea swell and prone to storm damage (part of the reason Trajan later built the sheltered hexagonal basin inland of it), but the basin itself, its moles, and surrounding quays were still functioning port infrastructure in 117 CE, working alongside Trajan's newer basin. Coordinates mark the approximate center of the basin as reconstructed from excavation/LIDAR plans (Keay et al., Portus Project); exact mole outlines are better attested than this single representative point, so treat coordinates as approximate (±300 m).
sources: Simon Keay, Martin Millett, Kristian Strutt, Portus: An Archaeological Survey of the Port of Imperial Rome (British School at Rome, 2005)

properties.notes: Trajan's inland hexagonal harbor basin, roughly 32 ha in area and about 716 m across, dug inland (southeast) of the exposed Claudian basin and connected to it and to the Tiber by canals, giving ships a sheltered anchorage safe from the open-sea storms that had damaged Portus Claudii. Construction ran c. 100-112 CE; the basin and its surrounding warehouse quays were functional and in full operation well before Trajan's death, squarely extant and in active use at the 117 CE snapshot. Together with the older Claudian basin it formed 'Portus Augusti et Traiani Felicis.' Coordinates from Pleiades' place record for the Trajanic harbor.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. on Portus

properties.notes: Monumental lighthouse modeled on the Pharos of Alexandria, built on an artificial mole-top island at the seaward mouth of the Claudian basin as part of Claudius's harbor project; functioning and celebrated on Nero's sestertii minted for the harbor's 64 CE dedication (obverse/reverse harbor scene showing the lighthouse between the two curving moles). A functioning aid to navigation still in active use in 117 CE, guiding shipping into both the Claudian and the newer Trajanic basin. Later depicted again on coinage under Trajan and subsequent emperors. Exact structure position is reconstructed from excavation on the mole between the two basins; treat this point as approximate (±200-300 m) pending direct access to Portus Project survey plans.

properties.modern_location: Fiumicino, Italy, between Portus and Ostia
properties.notes: Artificial canal (c. 90 m wide) linking the Portus basins to the Tiber and the sea, cutting off the wedge of land between it and the river's main channel to create the Isola Sacra. Sources disagree on strict attribution: despite the name 'Fossa Traiana,' the canal's origin is tied to Claudius's flood-relief/harbor-access works of the 40s CE (an inscription of 46 CE mentions it), though tradition and its surviving name credit Trajan, whose hexagonal-basin project of c. 100-112 CE certainly reused, enlarged, and depended on it as the link to the Tiber and sea. Whichever emperor's work is emphasized, the canal was long-since dug and functioning by 117 CE. Medieval Fiumicino ('little river') preserves its name. Coordinates are an approximate midpoint of the canal's course between Portus and the river; low positional precision.

Judgment call, flagged per brief guardrail: a large (c. 2 ha), three-story administrative/residential complex on the east side of the hexagonal basin, used for imperial visits and by officials of the praefectus annonae (grain supply). Brick-stamp evidence (Portus Project fieldwork) dates it predominantly to the Trajanic period, built 112/114-120 CE, with renovations continuing under Hadrian and the Antonines -- i.e., construction spans across Trajan's 117 CE death and was not complete until c. 120. Set extant_117ce:false, treating it like the Pantheon/Mausoleum-of-Hadrian precedent in this file (major structure demonstrably under active construction at the snapshot moment, not certainly usable/finished). A case could reasonably be made the other way (majority of an 8-year build likely stood by year 5), so this is a genuine judgment call worth a second look.

properties.modern_location: Fiumicino, Italy, on the artificial island between Ostia and Portus
properties.notes: Port-workers' cemetery strung for roughly 1.5 km along the road linking Ostia and Portus, on the 'sacred island' created by the Fossa Traiana canal. Burials began in the later 1st century CE and the necropolis was in continuous, active use through the 2nd-4th centuries; predominantly freedmen, merchants, sailors, and craftsmen tied to the port economy, with a documented shift from cremation to inhumation over the period. Squarely in active use at 117 CE, though its best-known monumental tomb facades and the bulk of excavated structures date to the 2nd-early 3rd century expansion (Hadrianic-Severan), i.e. after this snapshot -- included here as an active, populated burial ground already established by 117, not for its later, more famous phase.

The civic and religious center of Ostia, at the crossing of the Decumanus Maximus and Cardo, in use since the late Republic and continuously monumentalized under the early Empire (Tiberius built the Temple of Rome and Augustus here; a Republican-era predecessor temple to the Capitoline triad also stood at the forum's north end). By 117 CE the forum was a fully developed civic square, though its most famous surviving monument -- the great brick Capitolium -- was still a few years from completion under Hadrian (see separate entry). Point marks the forum's approximate center.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 4-5

properties.name_english: Capitolium of Ostia (Temple of Jupiter, Juno, Minerva)
properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, north side of the Forum
properties.notes: Judgment call, verified carefully per brief: the large brick-built, marble-clad Capitolium visible today, on a high podium at the north end of the Forum, is a Hadrianic building dated to c. 120 CE -- after Trajan's death (8 Aug 117) and Hadrian's accession the same day. Set extant_117ce:false because the standing monument postdates the snapshot. However, it stands directly above an earlier cult building of the 1st century BCE (probably dedicated to the same Capitoline triad) which was itself built over an even older public structure -- so the site had *a* temple to Jupiter/Juno/Minerva at 117 CE, just not the one now visible; the Hadrianic rebuild was very likely already underway (Hadrian's building program at Ostia is well documented as beginning right at his accession) but not complete. Kept in the file per the guardrail (don't drop, flag clearly) rather than omitted.

properties.name_english: Temple of Rome and Augustus, Ostia
properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, south end of the Forum
properties.notes: Podium temple (c. 24.4 x 13.7 m) closing the south end of the Forum, built early in Tiberius's reign, shortly after Augustus's death and deification in 14 CE, as part of Tiberius's broader building program at Ostia (which also gave the town its first fully monumental forum). Only the opus-reticulatum substructure survives today, but the temple was a standing, functioning cult building at 117 CE, over a century old by the snapshot date.

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, behind the Theatre
properties.notes: Large colonnaded square behind Ostia's theatre, designed together with the theatre in the Augustan period; its double-row Doric portico was added under Claudius (mid-1st century CE), giving it the form -- rows of small rooms (stationes) opening off the colonnade, used as offices by roughly 40 shipping and trade guilds (navicularii, negotiantes) -- that was substantially in place by 117 CE. The black-and-white mosaics identifying individual guilds by trade/origin (grain shippers, Sardinian and North African traders, ropemakers, etc.) that make the site famous today were laid in overlapping phases from the later 1st into the 2nd century CE, so some of the surviving mosaic pavement likely postdates 117; the square, portico, and guild-office function were established well before then. A small central temple (deity uncertain -- Ceres, Annona, and the deified emperors have all been proposed) was added around the end of the 1st century CE, also pre-117.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 6

properties.notes: Ostia's theatre was built at the end of the 1st century BCE under Augustus (constructed by his son-in-law and deputy Agrippa), originally seating around 3,000. This Augustan-era theatre was the standing structure at 117 CE. Its well-known enlargement to c. 4,000 seats -- the brick-faced form visible today -- was begun under Commodus (r. 176-192 CE) and completed/dedicated under Septimius Severus and Caracalla per an inscription of 196 CE, all well after this snapshot; per the brief's instruction, only the original Augustan-phase theatre is treated as extant in 117 CE, not its later Severan-period form.

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, near the Decumanus Maximus
properties.notes: Verified carefully per brief instruction, and excluded from the 117 CE snapshot as a result: the famous mosaic-floored Baths of Neptune were a Hadrianic project, built c. 117-138 CE in a wave of renovation Hadrian promoted at Ostia, with masonry confirmed Hadrianic by brick stamps and an inauguration inscription dated to late December 138 or 139 CE (i.e. completed under Antoninus Pius). Construction essentially began at, or just after, the moment of this map's snapshot, so it is not counted as standing on 8 August 117. It replaced an earlier, late-1st-century CE bath complex from Domitian's reign on the same footprint (a large Domitianic cistern beneath the palaestra survives, reused/then abandoned when the Hadrianic baths were built) -- that Domitianic bath building, not the one usually meant by 'Baths of Neptune,' is what was actually standing on this spot in 117 CE, but it isn't independently well enough attested by name/plan to warrant its own separate entry. Kept per guardrail rather than dropped, with extant_117ce:false and this explanation.

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, near the Forum
properties.notes: Ostia's largest and most important grain warehouse, with storage capacity for an estimated 6,000 metric tons of grain (about a year's dole for 16,000 people). Original construction begun under Claudius (reign 41-54 CE) -- identifiable by the characteristic rough-faced opus rusticum tufa-block east and west walls -- with expansion under Nero. That Julio-Claudian building, central to Rome's grain-supply chain (annona), was standing and in active use at 117 CE. It was substantially rebuilt in brick with an added first floor and extra storage cells in a later phase spanning the late 2nd-early 3rd centuries CE (Commodan/Severan), which postdates this snapshot and is not what's being marked extant here.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 15

properties.notes: One of Ostia's oldest surviving warehouses, built around a large tufa-columned courtyard with storage cellae, and traditionally attributed by name to a Lucius Hortensius (a fleet prefect at Misenum). Dating is genuinely a little uncertain and sources disagree: it is usually described as a late-Republican (1st century BCE) structure, but the earliest surviving masonry (opus reticulatum with sparse brick coursing) has independently been dated to roughly 25-50 CE, i.e. early Julio-Claudian rather than strictly Republican. Either dating puts it comfortably standing by 117 CE; the spread is noted here rather than resolved, per the brief's guidance to mark uncertainty rather than drop or fake precision.

Ostia's main east-west street, running from the Porta Romana through the Forum to the Porta Marina near the ancient shoreline, and continuing beyond the walls toward Rome as the Via Ostiensis. Its line goes back to the original castrum (fortified settlement, traditionally 4th century BCE, precise founding date disputed) and it remained the town's principal commercial and processional axis throughout antiquity, lined by shops, baths, and civic buildings by 117 CE. Point marks a representative location on the street near its crossing with the Cardo Maximus at the Forum, not the whole route (a single Point cannot represent a linear street; treat this as an anchor/label point only).
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 2

properties.notes: Northeastern gate of Ostia's Republican-era city walls, opening onto the Via Ostiensis toward Rome, at the start (from Rome's direction) of the Decumanus Maximus. The larger walled circuit that replaced Ostia's original small castrum is generally dated to the late 2nd-early 1st century BCE (often attributed to Sulla's era, c. 87-82 BCE, though scholars note the Sullan attribution itself lacks hard proof); a statue of Minerva excavated at the site is associated with the gate's decoration. Definitely standing and in use as the city's principal landward entrance at 117 CE.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 2

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, southwest circuit, near the ancient shoreline
properties.notes: Southwestern gate of Ostia's Republican walls, where the Decumanus Maximus left the walled town toward the ancient coastline (the sea has since retreated several km from this point due to Tiber siltation). Belonged to the Republican-era wall circuit, usually dated to around the middle of the 1st century BCE; its remains lie at a lower level than the present Decumanus surface. In use as the city's seaward gate at 117 CE, before the Hadrianic-Antonine bath and residential district later built up outside it (Terme di Porta Marina, synagogue vicinity) reached its later monumental form.
sources: Russell Meiggs, Roman Ostia (Oxford, 2nd ed. 1973), ch. 2

properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, outside Porta Marina, near the ancient shoreline
properties.notes: Verified carefully per brief instruction -- this is a genuinely contested date, not a settled one. Excavator M. Floriani Squarciapino (1961 discovery, publishing through the 1960s-70s) argued for a purpose-built synagogue on this site as early as the reign of Claudius (41-54 CE), which would make it the oldest known synagogue building in Europe/the Diaspora. That early dating has been directly challenged: L. Michael White has argued the original structure was a private house only later converted for Jewish communal/synagogue use, with the building's clearest synagogue-specific features (aedicula for the Torah shrine, etc.) belonging to a 2nd-4th century remodeling; A. Runesson and others have offered further alternative readings. Given the live scholarly dispute (Squarciapino vs. White vs. Runesson, argued out in journals including Harvard Theological Review), confidence is kept low rather than asserting the Claudian date as fact -- but even under the more cautious readings, some structure at this location in communal/religious use by the local Jewish population is plausible by the early-to-mid 2nd century at the latest, so it is kept as extant_117ce:true with a wide date/confidence caveat rather than dropped, per the guardrail.
sources: L. Michael White, 'Synagogue and Society in Imperial Ostia: Archaeological and Epigraphic Evidence', Harvard Theological Review 90 (1997)
M. Floriani Squarciapino, excavation reports on the Ostia synagogue (1961-64)

properties.name_english: Baths of the Marine Gate (Terme di Porta Marina)
properties.modern_location: Ostia Antica, Italy, just outside Porta Marina
properties.notes: A second Ostia bath complex checked carefully for dating alongside the Baths of Neptune, and excluded for the same reason: construction of this large spa complex outside the Porta Marina began under Trajan around 110 CE but continued through Hadrian's entire reign, with a dedicatory inscription dated to December 138 or 139 CE (possibly the 'lavacrum Ostiense' mentioned in the Historia Augusta as a project of Antoninus Pius). Because it was demonstrably still an active construction site spanning the 117 CE snapshot and not completed/dedicated until roughly two decades later, it is marked extant_117ce:false rather than counted as standing infrastructure at Trajan's death, even though ground was broken in his reign.

The second, much larger forum-basilica complex, rebuilt on the site of a smaller Flavian-era predecessor (c. 70-80 CE, demolished c. 100 CE). At roughly 167m long the basilica was the largest Roman building north of the Alps, but excavation/dating work (Leadenhall Court excavations 1984-86; reassessed in Britannia) places its construction across c. 100-125 CE, with several sources giving a completion date around 122 CE -- plausibly timed to Hadrian's visit to Britain that year. At the moment of this snapshot (Trajan's death, Aug 117) it was very likely still an active building site, not a finished civic building, so marked extant_117ce:false on the same 'commissioned but unfinished' logic Shift 2 applied to the Pantheon. Point marks the Leadenhall Market/Gracechurch Street site of the basilica's east end.

A large official residence and administrative complex on the north bank of the Thames, built c. 80-100 CE, with offices, reception halls, private quarters and an ornamental pool; identified with the site now under Cannon Street station. Plausibly the residence/office of the governor of Britannia. Definitely standing and in continuous official use by 117 CE.

A stone-walled 'playing-card' fort (c. 220m x 215m, ~4.7ha) in the northwest corner of Londinium, garrisoning roughly 1,000 troops including the governor's ceremonial guard. Archaeological consensus (Grimes excavations 1947-68; Britannia journal, 'London's Hadrianic War') dates the stone fort to c. 120 CE, plausibly connected to Hadrian's AD 122 visit to the province -- i.e. built after Trajan's death. No securely attested earlier (timber) fort phase on this exact site predates 117 CE, so marked extant_117ce:false; kept on the map since it's one of the most significant military structures in Roman London and its absence at the snapshot moment is itself a notable fact about 117 CE Londinium (still an undefended civilian town).

The original Roman timber bridge across the Thames, close to the modern London Bridge site, around which Londinium's settlement first grew from c. 47-50 CE. Roman bridges at this crossing were periodically rebuilt in timber throughout the occupation, so the exact physical structure standing in 117 CE is not separately dated in the sources found this shift -- but a bridge at this crossing point is universally agreed to have been continuously in place and in use since the mid-1st century CE. Confidence kept low because of that structural-continuity uncertainty, not because the crossing's existence is in doubt. New 'bridge' category introduced (schema has no existing bridge entry); nothing in Map.tsx enforces a closed category enum.

One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World; construction begun under Ptolemy I Soter, completed under Ptolemy II Philadelphus (traditionally dated 247/246 BCE), on the island of Pharos at the harbor mouth. Described in detail by Pliny (who gives its architect, Sostratus of Cnidus) and Strabo. Still standing and functioning as an active lighthouse throughout the Roman imperial period at the 117 CE snapshot; it survived until a series of medieval earthquakes felled it between the 11th and 14th centuries CE (long after our snapshot). Point is the traditional site, now occupied by the 15th-century Qaitbay Citadel.

Founded under Ptolemy I/II as part of the royal Mouseion research institute in the Bruchion (royal quarter). Its status by 117 CE is genuinely contested and this entry follows the guardrail for ambiguous cases: the institution's academic prestige had already been damaged by Ptolemy VIII's purge of scholars (145 BCE) and a portion of its holdings/buildings burned during Caesar's siege in 48 BCE (Roman civil-war fire that spread from the docks) -- but ancient sources (e.g. Athenaeus, writing in the later 2nd century CE) still describe scholarly activity in Alexandria, so the institution had not vanished outright by 117. Additionally, Alexandria itself was significantly damaged in the Kitos War / Jewish diaspora revolt of 115-117 CE -- the revolt was suppressed by Trajan's general Marcius Turbo in August 117 CE, essentially the same month as Trajan's death -- and Cassius Dio records major destruction of temples and public buildings in the city during that fighting, though no source found this shift specifically ties Library/Mouseion buildings to that damage. Kept extant_117ce:true (the institution demonstrably still existed) but confidence low given the compounding uncertainty about the physical building's exact condition at the snapshot moment. Coordinates are an approximate representative point in the former royal quarter (no precisely excavated Mouseion structure survives); wider tolerance intended.

Great Greco-Egyptian temple to Serapis built under Ptolemy III Euergetes (r. 246-222 BCE), housing a 'daughter library' subordinate to the main Mouseion collection. Sited on Alexandria's only natural hill, in the Rhakotis quarter. Standing and functioning at 117 CE; it was later destroyed by a Christian mob in 391 CE under Theophilus of Alexandria -- well after this snapshot.

A roughly seven-stadia (c. 1,300m) mole/causeway built under Ptolemy I connecting the mainland to Pharos island, dividing Alexandria's harbor into the Great Harbor and the harbor of Eunostos. Functioned as both a dam and a road; still in use in 117 CE. Later silted up and built over, forming the base of the modern city's Ras el-Tin peninsula neighborhood, so its exact ancient course is only approximately reconstructable -- point marks the traditional midpoint. Used 'road' as the closest existing category rather than adding a new one for a single feature.

Originally cut into the west slope of Panayır Dağ (Mt Pion) in the Hellenistic period (c. 200 BCE), the theatre was progressively enlarged in the Roman period: the stage building (scaenae frons) was completed under Nero (by 66 CE), the north analemma wall added under Domitian (92 CE), and the south analemma completed under Trajan (102-114 CE) -- meaning the theatre reached essentially its final, largest form (142m diameter, capacity c. 24,000) only shortly before the 117 CE snapshot. Definitely standing and in active use at Trajan's death.

Funerary library commissioned by Tiberius Julius Aquila (consul 110 CE) in honor of his father Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, a former proconsul of Asia; Celsus is entombed in a sarcophagus beneath the structure. Construction began c. 110 CE. Completion date is genuinely disputed in the sources found this shift: some (including several tourism/reference sites) state the building was 'completed in 117 CE,' but the more detailed accounts note Aquila himself died before the project finished and it was completed by his heirs, with the facade's full sculptural decoration not finished until c. 135 CE under Hadrian. Given that split and following the same cautious 117-snapshot logic Shift 2 applied to the Pantheon (a monument documented as 'still under construction' at Trajan's death even when some popular sources round its completion to the nearer date), this entry is marked extant_117ce:false -- the building was very plausibly still an active, unfinished construction/decoration site at the exact moment of the snapshot. A future shift with better access to Hueber/Thür's excavation publications should revisit this call.

One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The temple burned in 356 BCE (in a fire ancient writers synchronized with Alexander the Great's birth) and was rebuilt on an even grander scale over the following century, with the reconstruction generally dated complete by the mid-3rd century BCE. That Hellenistic-era structure -- described in detail by Pliny -- remained standing and was a major pilgrimage/cult site throughout the Roman period, including at 117 CE; it was eventually destroyed by a Gothic raid in 268 CE, well after this snapshot. Coordinates match the point already present in this repo's places_medium.geojson gazetteer for consistency.

Small but richly decorated temple on Curetes Street dedicated to (and named for) the emperor Hadrian. Because Hadrian's reign only began with his accession in August 117 CE -- the very event that closes this map's snapshot -- a temple dedicated in his honor cannot, under any dating given in the sources found this shift (which range from shortly after 117 to as late as the 130s CE), have existed at the 117 CE moment itself. Marked extant_117ce:false on that basis; kept on the map per the brief's guidance to record commissioned/imminent structures with the caveat explained, since it is one of Ephesus's best-known surviving Roman monuments and its story is directly tied to the exact turning point this whole map is built around.

Archaic Doric temple built c. 560 BCE, one of the oldest stone temples in mainland Greece; seven of its original 38 monolithic limestone columns still stand. It survived the Roman sack of Corinth under Mummius in 146 BCE and remained a landmark when Julius Caesar refounded the city as Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis in 44 BCE, still dominating the Roman forum in 117 CE. Pausanias (writing mid-2nd century CE, i.e. shortly after this snapshot) describes it standing over the marketplace.

Monumental spring-fed fountain house at the heart of Roman Corinth, immediately north of the Bema (rostra); one of the city's principal water sources since the Archaic period, associated in myth with the winged horse Pegasus. The elaborate two-story marble facade famously attributed to Herodes Atticus is a Antonine-era remodel (c. 150s CE, well after this snapshot) -- a simpler Hellenistic/early-Roman fountain house occupied the site and was functioning at 117 CE. New 'fountain' category introduced this shift; no closed enum enforced elsewhere in the app.

Roman civic basilica at the east end of the Corinthian forum/agora, dedicated to the Julio-Claudian imperial family and generally dated to the late 1st century BCE/early 1st century CE building phase of the refounded Roman colony. Standing and in use by 117 CE as part of the forum's administrative complex.

Panhellenic sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus east of Corinth, seat of the biennial Isthmian Games (one of the four Panhellenic 'crown' games), administered by Corinth throughout the Roman period. The Archaic temple (c. 690 BCE) burned in 470 BCE and was rebuilt; the sanctuary remained active and the games continued to be celebrated under Roman rule, including at 117 CE. Coordinates reuse the 'Isthmia' point already present in this repo's places_medium.geojson gazetteer for consistency.

Built at the foot of the Croix-Rousse hill, at the historical confluence of the Rhône and Saône, funded by C. Julius Rufus (a priest of the imperial cult) per a surviving dedicatory inscription (CIL XIII 1698) dated 19 CE; it was the site of the annual Concilium Galliarum, the federal assembly of the 'Three Gauls' provinces. Enlarged early in the 2nd century CE with two added galleries, raising capacity to roughly 20,000 -- the precise date of that expansion relative to 117 CE was not pinned down this shift, so it is noted here rather than asserted either way, but the core 19 CE amphitheatre was unambiguously standing and in use at the 117 CE snapshot regardless.

Built into the slope of the Fourvière hill (site of the original Roman colonia founded 43 BCE) under Augustus, c. 15 BCE, with a capacity of roughly 10,000; enlarged under Hadrian later in the 2nd century. Definitely standing and in use as of 117 CE, prior to the Hadrianic enlargement.

properties.name_english: Federal Altar / Sanctuary of the Three Gauls
properties.notes: Altar to the cult of Roma and Augustus dedicated in 12 BCE at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône, the ritual and political center of the Concilium Galliarum -- the annual gathering of representatives from the 60 civitates of the Three Gauls to elect the high priest of the imperial cult (the first was Gaius Julius Vercondaridubnus, an Aeduan) and celebrate games. Continuously in use throughout the early Empire, including 117 CE. Located adjacent to (and administratively linked with) the Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls built nearby a generation later; exact footprint of the altar precinct itself is only approximately reconstructed archaeologically, hence medium rather than high confidence on the point location.

The longest of Lugdunum's four aqueducts (c. 86km, from the Gier valley near Saint-Chamond), famous for the Beaunant and Chaponost inverted-siphon sections. Its dating has been a long-running scholarly controversy: early lead-pipe evidence pointed to Claudius (mid-1st c. CE), an 1887 inscription (the 'pierre de Chagnon') pointed to Hadrian, and a 1982 find of a Claudian-dedication fountain pointed back to Claudius again. A 2018 dendrochronological study of the Beaunant bridge-siphon's timber foundations dated them to 110 CE, placing the engineering work under Trajan with 'possible finalization under Hadrian' per the excavators. Given that direct physical dating (110 CE, seven years before this snapshot) and absent evidence the system was non-functional at 117, this entry is kept extant_117ce:true, but confidence is set low given how contested the aqueduct's dating remains in the literature -- a future shift with direct access to the Revue archéologique de l'Est article should revisit. Point marks the well-preserved Chaponost arcade section.

Built between 5 and 1 BCE under the patronage of Augustus's heirs Gaius and Lucius Caesar (named in the dedicatory inscription), seating c. 6,000; rediscovered beneath the old town only in 1988. Standing and in use at 117 CE.

Part temple, part college for the imperial cult, built as part of Augustus's extensive redesign of Carthago Nova alongside its new forum, streets and theatre; sits within the Molinete hill archaeological park in the heart of the old town. Exact construction date within the Augustan period and full identification of the structure's function are still debated in the Spanish excavation literature, hence medium confidence, but the building's Augustan-era existence and continuity into the 2nd century CE are not in dispute.

Civic and religious center of the Augustan-refounded colony, on the Molinete hill; excavated and now presented in the Molinete Roman Forum Museum. Established as part of the same 1st-century BCE/CE urban redevelopment as the theatre and Augusteum, standing at 117 CE.

Not a single structure but the vast silver-and-lead mining district in the hills immediately east of the city, worked intensively from the Carthaginian period (Hasdrubal and Hannibal both drew on its silver from the 220s BCE) and massively expanded under Rome; Strabo (writing around the turn of the era) reports roughly 40,000 workers, mostly enslaved, active in the mines. This revenue was a primary reason Carthago Nova mattered to Rome and remained a major economic engine of Hispania Tarraconensis through the 2nd century CE. Point is a representative centroid of the Sierra Minera de Cartagena-La Unión district, not a single excavated site -- confidence marked low and coordinates should be read as 'somewhere across this district' per the brief's guidance for wide-tolerance features.

One of the largest circuses in the Roman world (over 490m long, capacity up to c. 80,000), modeled on the Circus Maximus. Its founding date is debated in the sources found this shift (a first structure c. 50 BCE, with substantial rebuilding credited to Trajan's reign, 98-117 CE), but its existence and use by 117 CE is directly attested by a primary source: Cassius Dio (68.25) records that Trajan himself took shelter in the circus during the catastrophic Antioch earthquake of 13 December 115 CE, escaping through a window as aftershocks continued for days. The earthquake (est. M7.5, Mercalli X-XI) caused near-total destruction across the city and killed an estimated tens of thousands; Antioch -- one of the four largest cities of the empire -- was still very much in a state of post-earthquake reconstruction at the moment of this map's 117 CE snapshot, only about 20 months later.

A theatre 'under the rocks of Silpius' is attributed by ancient sources to works undertaken during Julius Caesar's visits to the city (mid-1st century BCE); it was expanded by later emperors. The site has not been excavated, so its precise location and condition are not well documented -- coordinates here are approximate, on the flank of Mt Silpius above the city center. Kept extant_117ce:true since there is no evidence the structure ceased to exist, but flagged low confidence for two compounding reasons: the imprecise location, and the fact that Antioch was still recovering from the devastating December 115 CE earthquake (see Circus of Antioch entry) at the moment of this snapshot, so the theatre's exact condition in 117 specifically is uncertain even though the building itself was not newly destroyed or newly built in that window.

Famous oracular sanctuary and sacred grove of Apollo and Artemis at Daphne, a suburb roughly 8km southwest of Antioch, established alongside the city's founding tradition under Seleucus I (c. 300 BCE) and described by Strabo as one of the most celebrated sanctuaries of the ancient world. A major pilgrimage and recreational site throughout the Roman period, including 117 CE. Point uses the same Harbiye/Daphne location already present in this repo's places_medium.geojson gazetteer for consistency.

Residence and administrative seat of the governor of Germania Inferior, its remains (including a sewer system) lie beneath Cologne's medieval/modern city hall (Rathaus); recent MiQua excavations near the site uncovered a 1st-century staircase and later building phases. Originally built as army headquarters for the Lower Rhine command, it became the governor's palace once Germania Inferior was formally organized as a province (83/84 CE). Standing and functioning as the seat of provincial government at 117 CE. Exact original 1st-century construction phase/date is not precisely fixed in the sources found this shift, hence medium confidence.

Roughly 4km circuit of stone fortification with at least 9 gates and 19 round towers, enclosing the colonia founded in 50 CE; construction is generally placed at the end of the 1st century CE (c. 89-91 CE). Standing and defining the city's built-up extent at 117 CE. New 'wall' category introduced this shift (parallels the London Wall case flagged in the backlog/SHIFT_LOG, which is deliberately NOT included here since it postdates 117 by nearly a century).

The oldest known stone structure in Cologne: a roughly 9x9m tuff-stone tower (originally c. 12m tall, c. 6m survive today) built on an oak-pile foundation dendrochronologically dated to the winter of 4/5 CE, marking the entrance to the Rhine harbor of the pre-colonia settlement (Oppidum Ubiorum). It was partly demolished when the later stone city wall was built (c. 90 CE), so what stood at 117 CE was already a reduced remnant of the original Augustan-era tower rather than the complete structure -- kept extant_117ce:true since a fragment did remain in place (consistent with what is visible on-site today), but confidence is low given the compounding uncertainty about exactly how much of it was still standing at the specific 117 CE moment.

A prosperous Campanian town of ~11,000-12,000 people at the mouth of the Sarno river, buried under ~4-6 m of pumice and ash in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius on 24-25 August 79 CE and never reoccupied. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's 117 CE snapshot — included as a general wayfinding/city-center pin so the site reads on the map even though nothing here was standing at Trajan's death; individual landmark pins carry the architectural detail. Point marks a representative centroid near the Forum.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16 and 6.20 (to Tacitus, eyewitness account of the eruption)

properties.notes: The rectangular civic, religious, and commercial heart of Pompeii, laid out by the 2nd century BCE and ringed by the Capitolium, Basilica, macellum, comitium, and temples of Apollo and the Genius of Augustus. Buried by the 79 CE eruption. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

Built c. 70 BCE at private expense by local magistrates Gaius Quinctius Valgus and Marcus Porcius shortly after Pompeii became a Roman colony (80 BCE); it is the oldest known permanent stone amphitheatre in the Roman world, predating the Colosseum by roughly 150 years, and held about 20,000 spectators. Buried by the eruption of 79 CE. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.
sources: Tacitus, Annales 14.17 (the 59 CE riot between Pompeian and Nucerian spectators at this amphitheatre)

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy (north end of the Forum)
properties.notes: Founded in the second half of the 2nd century BCE, originally dedicated to Jupiter alone; after Pompeii became a Roman colony in 80 BCE it was reconsecrated as a Capitolium to the triad Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, closing the north end of the Forum. Badly damaged in the earthquake of 62 CE and still unrepaired when the 79 CE eruption buried it. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.
sources: Seneca, Naturales Quaestiones 6.1 (on the 62 CE earthquake damage to Pompeii's public buildings)

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy (west side of the Forum)
properties.notes: Pompeii's oldest and most important religious sanctuary, with cult origins reaching back to the 6th century BCE under Greek/Etruscan influence; the present colonnaded form dates to a 2nd-century BCE rebuild, with further repairs under way after the 62 CE earthquake, still incomplete in 79 CE. Bronze statues of Apollo and Diana found here are now in the Naples Archaeological Museum. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy (southwest corner of the Forum)
properties.notes: Built c. 130-120 BCE, this is among the oldest surviving basilicas anywhere in the Roman world, predating the amphitheatre by several decades. It served as Pompeii's law court and a covered meeting hall for business, with a raised two-story tribunal at its western end. Buried in 79 CE. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy (corner of Via Stabiana and Via dell'Abbondanza)
properties.notes: The oldest and largest of Pompeii's public bath complexes, with an original core going back to the 2nd century BCE (some scholars trace earlier phases to the 4th century BCE); enlarged repeatedly, it only received piped aqueduct water around the turn of the 1st century CE, having previously relied on a well and roof-catchment reservoir. Buried by the 79 CE eruption. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy (Theatre District, adjoining the Triangular Forum)
properties.notes: A stone theatre cut into a natural hillside slope in the Samnite/Hellenistic tradition, with an original phase as early as the 3rd century BCE and a major 2nd-century BCE rebuild; seated roughly 5,000. Renovated again under Augustus at the private expense of the Holconius brothers. Buried by the 79 CE eruption. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

One of the largest and best-preserved private houses in Pompeii, c. 1,100 sq m, originally built in the 2nd century BCE and lavishly redecorated in the elaborate Fourth Style after the 62 CE earthquake for its owners, the freedmen brothers Aulus Vettius Restitutus and Aulus Vettius Conviva. Sealed under ash in 79 CE with its frescoes almost intact, making it one of the most-studied domus in the Roman world. New category "house" introduced for this feature (domus) since none of the existing categories fit a private residence; logged per shift convention of introducing categories freely. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy, c. 400 m northwest of the walls near the Herculaneum Gate
properties.notes: A suburban villa just outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, built in the 1st century BCE and famous for the near-life-size Dionysiac frieze (c. 60 BCE) painted around its triclinium (Room 5), thought to depict a woman's initiation into a mystery cult of Dionysus/Bacchus. Because it lay outside the town walls it took relatively light structural damage in 79 CE, which is why its frescoes survive so completely. New category "villa" introduced (distinct from in-town "house") for this and the Villa of the Papyri entry, following the shift log's precedent of adding categories freely. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Pompei, Campania, Italy (west edge of the city walls)
properties.notes: One of Pompeii's seven city gates, on the western wall near the ancient shoreline, connecting the town to its harbor and the Bay of Naples; its double-arched, barrel-vaulted form (a wide arch for animals/carts, a narrow one for pedestrians) is largely a Sullan-colony-era (post-80 BCE) rebuild of an older opening in the Samnite walls. Buried in 79 CE and not fully excavated until 1861 under Giuseppe Fiorelli. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

A smaller, wealthier seaside town of perhaps 4,000-5,000 people on a coastal spur of Vesuvius, about 8 km southeast of Neapolis. Spared the initial ash-fall that struck Pompeii (giving most residents time to flee toward the shore) but destroyed the following night and morning by a series of pyroclastic surges and flows that buried the town up to 20 m deep, carbonizing (rather than burning away) organic material — wood, food, papyrus, even some human tissue — far more completely than at Pompeii. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as a general wayfinding/city-center pin, same reasoning as the Pompeii city pin.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae 6.16 and 6.20 (to Tacitus)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-32623-3 (Scientific Reports, 2023, on the pyroclastic surge sequence at Herculaneum)

properties.notes: Meeting hall and shrine of the Augustales, a civic college mostly of wealthy freedmen tasked with maintaining the imperial cult of Augustus (the priesthood was formalized under Tiberius in 14 CE, though this building's core dates slightly earlier, funded by patrons A. Lucius Proculus and A. Lucius Iulianus). Decorated with Fourth-Style frescoes of the labors of Hercules, the city's mythic founder. Rediscovered in 1740 by early Bourbon tunnel excavations. New category "collegium" introduced since this is a civic/cult association's meeting hall rather than a standalone temple; logged per shift convention. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Ercolano, Campania, Italy (south edge of town, near the ancient shoreline)
properties.notes: Built in the early 1st century CE as a gift to the town by its greatest benefactor, Marcus Nonius Balbus (ex-tribune, ex-consul, ex-proconsul of Crete), who split the complex off from his own adjoining residence; damaged in the 62 CE earthquake and subsequently expanded with an open-air pool and nymphaeum. Widely regarded as the best-preserved Roman bath building anywhere, buried by the 79 CE pyroclastic flows and only fully excavated/opened in the 20th-21st centuries. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.name_english: House of the Deer (Casa dei Cervi)
properties.modern_location: Ercolano, Campania, Italy (Insula IV, near the ancient shoreline)
properties.notes: The grandest excavated house in Herculaneum, a two-story waterfront residence built/rebuilt under Claudius (41-54 CE) and expanded by absorbing a neighboring property; named for two marble sculptures of deer attacked by hounds found in its garden, and noted for well-preserved still-life frescoes. Street-facing rooms were converted to shops after the 62 CE earthquake. Fully uncovered by Amedeo Maiuri's open-air excavations of 1929-1932. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

properties.modern_location: Ercolano, Campania, Italy, northwest of the main excavated town, mostly still unexcavated/underground
properties.notes: A vast luxury villa on the coast northwest of the town center, plausibly linked (unconfirmed) to Julius Caesar's father-in-law L. Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus; famous for its library of over 1,800 carbonized papyrus scrolls, discovered by Bourbon tunneling from 1750, mostly Epicurean philosophical texts including many works of Philodemus of Gadara. COORDINATE/EXTENT CAUTION: only a fraction of the villa has ever been excavated (much still lies under modern Ercolano and below the water table), so its full footprint and this point's precision are both genuinely uncertain — the coordinates mark the excavated atrium/peristyle area reached by 18th-century tunnels and 20th-century open-air digs, not a confirmed full-villa centroid. Destroyed in the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius, 38 years before this map's snapshot — included as it's an essential part of the story.

Legio I Adiutrix ('Loyal and Faithful'), raised by Nero/Galba from Ravenna fleet marines in 68 CE, was moved from Moguntiacum (Mainz) to Pannonia c. 86-92 CE under Domitian and Brigetio became its long-term home (into the 4th c.). CAVEAT: the legion fought in Trajan's Dacian and Parthian Wars (101-106, 114-117), and multiple sources state it was 'sent back to Pannonia, with base in Brigetio' specifically by Hadrian after Trajan's death (r. from 8 Aug 117) — meaning that at the exact 117 CE snapshot the legion itself was very likely still with the field army in the East (Syria/Mesopotamia/Cappadocia, exact camp unattested) or in transit, only physically reoccupying Brigetio c. 118 CE. Brigetio's garrison in 117 CE proper was Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix (see separate entry), which held the fortress from 105 until it ceded it to the returning I Adiutrix and moved to Vetera in 122. Pinned here as I Adiutrix's essentially-continuous permanent fortress (pre- and post-Parthian War) with the transfer gap flagged.
sources: https://www.livius.org/articles/legion/legio-i-adiutrix/ (cross-referenced via search synthesis, direct fetch blocked)

properties.notes: Legio I Minervia was levied by Domitian in 82-83 CE for the Chattian War and based at Bonna (Bonn) from its founding; it remained the legion's home fortress for the rest of its existence (with a brief detachment fighting for Trajan in the Dacian Wars). The legion's legate c. 101-106 CE was the future emperor Hadrian. By 117 CE the legion had long since returned to and was firmly garrisoned at Bonna.

Legio I Italica, raised by Nero in 66-67 CE from Italian recruits, was posted to Novae on the lower Danube by Vespasian in 69-70 CE and remained there for the rest of its long service (into the 5th century). Its timber-and-earth camp was rebuilt in stone during the Trajanic period (98-117 CE), so by the 117 CE snapshot the legion occupied a substantially stone fortress. Detachments served in Trajan's Dacian and Parthian campaigns, but the main base stayed at Novae throughout.

Legio II Adiutrix, like I Adiutrix raised from fleet marines (68-70 CE), fought in Trajan's Dacian Wars based temporarily at Singidunum, then was permanently transferred to Aquincum in 106 CE once the new province of Pannonia Inferior was organized, becoming that province's senior garrison and the anchor of what grew into Aquincum's civilian town (later Pannonia Inferior's capital). Its earlier wood-and-earth camp was under stone reconstruction during Hadrian's reign, begun essentially at the 117 CE snapshot.

Legio II Augusta, one of Claudius's original invasion legions of 43 CE, moved to a new purpose-built fortress at Isca Silurum (Caerleon) in South Wales c. 74-75 CE under governor Sextus Julius Frontinus, replacing timber defenses in stone c. 99-100 CE per a Trajanic building inscription. The legion was still garrisoned there in 117 CE and would remain for roughly two more centuries.

properties.name_english: Camp of Legio II Traiana Fortis (Judaea)
properties.modern_location: Kefar 'Otnay / Legio junction, near Megiddo, Israel
properties.notes: Legio II Traiana Fortis was raised by Trajan c. 101-105 CE for the Dacian Wars and fought in his Parthian campaign (114-117). Multiple sources place it 'in Iudaea, to ensure peace' specifically in 117 CE, immediately after the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt (115-117) — i.e. present in the same province, and very plausibly the same Jezreel Valley camp at Caparcotna/Legio, as VI Ferrata (see that entry) during this transitional year. GENUINE UNCERTAINTY: the legion's permanent post-117 home was Nicopolis near Alexandria, Egypt, but sources disagree on whether it arrived there by c. 119-120 or only by 125 CE. Pinned here at the Judaean camp for the 117 CE snapshot specifically, distinct from its later Egyptian base (not shown, since it postdates 117).

CORRECTION TO INITIAL BRIEF: III Augusta's base in 117 CE was Lambaesis, not Theveste. The legion was transferred from Ammaedara to Theveste under Vespasian (75 CE), then Trajan relocated it further into the Aurès foothills to Lambaesis c. 100 CE for better control of Berber/Musulamian tribal territory — a full generation before 117. The famous monumental stone camp visible today (and Hadrian's personal 128 CE address to the assembled troops, recorded on the 'Adlocutio' inscription) reflects a Hadrianic rebuilding in stone (123-129 CE) of an already-occupied Trajanic-era timber/earth base, so the legion was present at Lambaesis, just not yet in its famous stone form, at the 117 CE snapshot.

Legio III Cyrenaica moved from Egypt to garrison the newly annexed province of Arabia (106 CE) after Trajan's peaceful annexation of the Nabataean kingdom, founding a fortress at Bostra, the new provincial capital. GENUINE UNCERTAINTY FOR THE 117 CE SNAPSHOT: sources indicate the legion (or a large detachment) was pulled back to Egypt around 116-117 CE to help suppress the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt, is attested together with XXII Deiotariana in Egypt in 119 CE, and only clearly returned to Bostra c. 120-127 CE. It is therefore genuinely unclear whether the legion's main body was physically at Bostra or in Egypt at the exact moment of Trajan's death in August 117. Pinned at Bostra as its official provincial post (both immediately before and after this disruption).

Legio III Gallica, an old Caesarian-era legion long stationed in Syria, was based at Raphanaea (modern Rafniye) in the Orontes valley through the late Republic and into the imperial period, continuing under Trajan and Hadrian. The site is only lightly excavated (limited visible remains, walled-enclosure traces from 1930s aerial survey), so the coordinate is a settlement-level approximation rather than an excavated principia point.

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio IV Flavia Felix (Singidunum)
properties.notes: Legio IV Flavia Felix was raised by Vespasian in 70 CE from the cadre of the disbanded IV Macedonica, and was moved to Singidunum (modern Belgrade) by Domitian in 86 CE to shore up the Danube frontier after the Dacian invasion that destroyed V Alaudae. It remained Singidunum's garrison through 117 CE and for centuries after (into the 5th century).

Legio IV Scythica was stationed at Zeugma, guarding the strategic Euphrates crossing on the Syria-Parthia frontier, from 66 CE onward for roughly a century, including through Trajan's Parthian War (114-117), in which the legion took part. Recent excavation (Zeugma archaeological project) places the actual legionary camp on the plateau west of the town proper (the 'Meydani' sector), rather than directly on the riverbank city site itself; the point given here marks the town/site as commonly plotted, with that camp-vs-town nuance noted.

Legio V Macedonica, veteran of Trajan's Dacian Wars, was transferred to Troesmis on the lower Danube in 107 CE to guard against the Roxolani Sarmatians and the Black Sea Greek cities' hinterland. It remained based there through 117 CE and until the 160s, though a vexillation was sent east for Trajan's Parthian campaign (115-117).

Legio VI Ferrata was brought into Judaea as its second permanent legion (alongside X Fretensis at Jerusalem) in the aftermath of the Kitos War, founding a camp on a hill above the Jezreel Valley near Kefar 'Otnay/Caparcotna (which gave the later settlement its name, 'Legio', and eventually modern Lajjun/Megiddo). Sources consistently cite 117 CE for this establishment, though the user's brief flags — and archaeological/epigraphic work (Tel Aviv University/Jezreel Valley Regional Project excavations) leaves open — that the stone fortress construction and full garrison strength may date slightly later, c. 117-120 CE, into Hadrian's reign. May have briefly overlapped in the area with II Traiana Fortis (see separate entry) during this same transitional year before that legion moved on toward Egypt.

Legio VI Victrix moved from its older camp at Novaesium (Neuss) to the single-legion fortress Vetera II near Xanten around the turn of the 1st/2nd century CE, and was still garrisoned there in 117 CE, forming (with X Gemina) the backbone of the lower Rhine defense. It stayed at Vetera II until 122 CE, when Hadrian personally brought it to Britain to help build Hadrian's Wall, at which point XXX Ulpia Victrix took over Vetera II — a transfer that postdates this map's 117 CE snapshot, so VI Victrix (not XXX Ulpia Victrix) is the correct 117 CE occupant of this site.

Legio VII Claudia had been in the Moesian theatre since the mid-1st century and became the fixed garrison and namesake military anchor of Viminacium once Domitian split Moesia into two provinces in 86 CE, with Viminacium as Moesia Superior's capital and governor's seat. The legion was still there in 117 CE (Viminacium was elevated toward municipium status right around Hadrian's accession) and remained for centuries.

Legio VIII Augusta was permanently stationed at Argentorate (Strasbourg), guarding a key Rhine crossing, from c. 90 CE and remained there for over three centuries. By 117 CE the fortress's defenses were being reinforced as part of Hadrian's broader consolidation of the German limes.

Legio IX Hispana founded the legionary fortress at Eboracum (York) in 71 CE and was recorded rebuilding it in stone in 107-108 CE. It was still based there in 117 CE; a later, much-debated tradition (going back to Mommsen) has the legion wiped out fighting a Brigantian/Caledonian uprising around 117-120 CE, but this is now widely doubted — inscriptions from Nijmegen suggest elements of IX Hispana were redeployed to the Rhine by c. 120 CE rather than destroyed, with the legion's actual disappearance from the record more plausibly explained by later events (a Rhine posting, or loss during the Parthian War of Lucius Verus or the Bar Kokhba Revolt). FLAGGED PER BRIEF: this entry reflects only the well-attested 117 CE status (still garrisoned at York); its subsequent fate is a genuine, unresolved scholarly dispute, not a 117 CE fact.

Legio X Fretensis garrisoned the ruins of Jerusalem continuously from the city's destruction in 70 CE, encamped on the southwestern hill (the former Herodian Upper City), incorporating the Phasael/Hippicus/Mariamne towers of Herod's palace into its camp wall. It was still Jerusalem's sole legionary garrison in 117 CE; the refoundation of the city as the colony Aelia Capitolina is usually dated c. 130 CE under Hadrian (one late source, Epiphanius, gives 117, but mainstream scholarship treats that as a chronological error), so at the 117 CE snapshot this is still a legionary camp on Jerusalem's ruins, not yet the colonia.

properties.modern_location: Vienna city center (Hoher Markt area), Austria
properties.notes: Legio X Gemina, long stationed at Noviomagus (Nijmegen) in Germania Inferior (71-103 CE), was transferred east to Aquincum in 103 CE and then to a new permanent fortress at Vindobona (Vienna) in 114 CE, where it remained the garrison through 117 CE and for centuries afterward, anchoring the Danube frontier opposite the Marcomanni and Quadi.

Legio XI Claudia was transferred to Durostorum on the lower Danube between 104 and 114 CE (sources vary on the exact year within that window, but agree it predates 117), evacuating Brigetio for XXX Ulpia Victrix in the process. It remained Durostorum's garrison through 117 CE and for roughly three more centuries, guarding the Danube against the Getae/Roxolani.

Legio XII Fulminata was posted to Melitene on the upper Euphrates after the First Jewish-Roman War (from 71-72 CE), guarding the crossing into Armenia and the end of the road east from Caesarea. It took part in Trajan's Armenian campaign (114) and remained based at Melitene through 117 CE and for centuries after (attested there in the Notitia Dignitatum).

Legio XIII Gemina stayed behind in the newly conquered province after Trajan's Second Dacian War, founding its fortress at Apulum (modern Alba Iulia) in 106-108 CE and becoming the senior garrison of the new province. It remained Dacia's principal legion through 117 CE, even as sub-units were pulled for Trajan's simultaneous Parthian campaign (115-117).

Legio XIV Gemina was sent to Pannonia in 92 CE to replace the destroyed XXI Rapax, initially camping at Vindobona, then relocated to Carnuntum after Trajan's Dacian Wars. Sources vary on the precise year of the Carnuntum move (given variously as 106, 114, or 117-118), but agree the legion was there by, or essentially at, the 117 CE snapshot and remained for the next three centuries as the provincial capital's garrison and headquarters of the Pannonian fleet.

Legio XV Apollinaris fought in Trajan's Parthian War (114-117) and was in Egypt in the war's immediate aftermath; scholarship on its movements (Speidel) dates its departure for its new permanent post at Satala, on the Cappadocian-Armenian frontier, to around August 117 CE (i.e., essentially at Trajan's death/Hadrian's accession), arriving and establishing its castrum stativum there by summer 118. At the exact 117 CE snapshot the legion was thus most likely already marching toward, or just arriving at, Satala rather than fully garrisoned in its permanent stone fortress — flagged accordingly.

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio XX Valeria Victrix (Chester)
properties.notes: Deva was first built by Legio II Adiutrix c. 70 CE, but II Adiutrix left Britain in the mid-80s and Legio XX Valeria Victrix took over the fortress c. 88 CE, rebuilding it in stone. XX Valeria Victrix remained Deva's garrison through 117 CE and for the following two centuries.

properties.modern_location: Sidi Gaber area, east Alexandria, Egypt
properties.notes: Legio XXII Deiotariana (descended from client-king Deiotarus of Galatia's forces, absorbed by Augustus) was one of Egypt's two permanent legions, based with III Cyrenaica at the double-legion fortress of Nicopolis just east of Alexandria. Elements were used to suppress the Kitos War/Jewish diaspora revolt in Egypt and Cyrenaica (115-117), so the legion (or most of it) was in the immediate Alexandria area through 117 CE; it is attested there again with III Cyrenaica in 119. It was later destroyed or disbanded during the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132-136 CE), long after this map's snapshot. No visible remains of the fortress survive and its precise footprint is unexcavated, so the point is a settlement-level approximation.

Legio XXII Primigenia, raised by Caligula in 39 CE, was stationed at Mogontiacum (Mainz) from 92 CE onward (having shared earlier Rhine postings with other legions), guarding the Rhine and the Mainz bridge. It remained Mainz's garrison through 117 CE and for the following two centuries; the future emperor Hadrian served as one of its military tribunes in 97-98 CE.

properties.name_english: Fortress of Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix (Brigetio)
properties.notes: CORRECTION TO INITIAL BRIEF: Legio XXX Ulpia Victrix's 117 CE base was Brigetio, not Vetera. The legion was raised by Trajan (c. 101-105 CE, sources vary) for the Dacian Wars and, once XI Claudia vacated Brigetio for Durostorum, took over that Pannonian fortress from 105 CE. It held Brigetio through the entire 117 CE snapshot and only moved to Vetera (Xanten) in 122 CE, when Hadrian sent VI Victrix (Vetera's prior occupant) to Britain and reassigned XXX Ulpia Victrix into the vacated fortress — coincidentally the same year Legio I Adiutrix returned from the East to reclaim Brigetio (see that entry's note on the same swap).

Misenum was home to the classis Misenensis, the senior fleet of the Roman navy, founded by Augustus in 27 BCE to command the western Mediterranean. Up to 10,000 sailors and marines were based on the peninsula, drawing fresh water from the vast vaulted cistern known as the Piscina Mirabilis. Pliny the Elder commanded the fleet from here in 79 CE and sailed from this harbor to his death during the eruption of Vesuvius. In 2023 archaeologists uncovered a monumental harborside villa believed to belong to the fleet's prefect.

Classe was the harbor of the classis Ravennas, the second of Augustus's two main Italian fleets, guarding the Adriatic. The base held up to 250 ships and 10,000 marines, linked to Ravenna itself and to the Po by the Fossa Augusta canal, with naval yards and docks stretching some 22 kilometers along the waterway. Silting has since pushed the coastline nine kilometers east of the ancient shoreline.

Forum Iulii's stone harbor, nicknamed Claustra Maris or Sea Bolt, was built by Octavian after Actium as a third great naval base alongside Misenum and Ravenna, guarding the northwest Mediterranean. Its fleet, the classis Gallica, stayed active through the Julio-Claudian era but lost its standing amid the civil wars of 69 CE, after which its ships were reassigned toward Misenum and the Adriatic. The hexagonal harbor basin, once ringed by warehouses and now landlocked more than a kilometer from the sea, still survives as the Lanterne d'Auguste monument marking its ancient entrance.

The classis Alexandrina was established after Actium to guard Rome's most vital grain route, escorting the Alexandrian corn fleet across the Mediterranean and patrolling the Nile. Its ships moored in the Great Harbor below the royal quarter on the Lochias peninsula, close by the Pharos lighthouse that already marked the port for the ancient world.

Seleucia Pieria served as the seaport of Antioch and home of the classis Syriaca, the Roman navy's main eastern fleet. Vespasian rebuilt the harbor around 70 CE with an inner and outer basin fed by a canal cut partly through solid rock, a feat of engineering still visible today as the Titus Tunnel, designed to flush silt from the port entrance.

Gesoriacum was the Channel headquarters of the classis Britannica, the fleet Claudius built to launch and then supply the conquest of Britain from 43 CE onward. The fortified port sat on the cliff above the Liane estuary, doubling as the customs post for cross-Channel trade and the usual embarkation point for emperors and officials bound for Britannia.

The Alteburg fort on a low bluff south of Cologne was the headquarters of the classis Germanica, the Rhine fleet and the largest of Rome's provincial navies. More than a thousand marines were garrisoned here to patrol the river from the Rhine-Meuse delta up past the legionary fortresses, keeping the frontier's supply lines and communications running.

Taurunum stood at the meeting of the Sava and Danube rivers and served as the main base of the classis Flavia Pannonica, the fleet that patrolled the upper and middle Danube from Regensburg down to Belgrade. Flotillas based here ferried troops and supplies to the string of forts along the river frontier.

Noviodunum guarded the last narrow crossing of the Danube before the river fans into its delta and the Black Sea beyond.
